# Concurrency {#sec-concurrency}

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("_common.R")
```

R runs code in parallel by running more R processes. The function `parallel::mclapply()` forks the current session into workers and collects what they return. Each worker starts from the session's memory, which the operating system shares between the processes until one of them changes it. Rust runs code in parallel with *threads*, which share one process and its memory. Sharing memory is faster than copying it, and it's also how data races happen: two threads using the same value at once without coordinating, at least one of them changing it. Rust's ownership and borrowing rules (@sec-ownership, @sec-borrowing) rule out data races at compile time. This chapter runs the same bootstrap in parallel with `mclapply()`, with threads from the standard library, and with the `rayon` crate [@rayon], and shows how Rust handles shared state. The matching chapter of the Rust book is "Fearless Concurrency" [@rustbook, chap. 16].

## A bootstrap to parallelize

The example bootstraps the maximum likelihood estimate from @sec-closures. It draws resamples of the seven values with replacement, fits the Cauchy location to each one, and takes the standard deviation of the estimates as a standard error.

Searching the whole interval once, as @sec-closures did, isn't enough for these fits. A resample that repeats the 15 can move the global minimum of the negative log-likelihood to near 15, while `optimize()` still returns the local one near 1.

So in R, `fit()` evaluates `nll` on a grid and refines the best grid point with `optimize()`:

```{r}
#| label: r-fit
make_nll <- function(x) {
  force(x)
  function(m) -sum(dcauchy(x, location = m, log = TRUE))
}
fit <- function(x) {
  nll <- make_nll(x)
  grid <- seq(-10, 20, by = 0.1)
  best <- grid[which.min(vapply(grid, nll, numeric(1)))]
  optimize(nll, c(best - 0.1, best + 0.1))$minimum
}
```

I split the work into four tasks of 250 resamples, each with its own seed, so a task's draws don't depend on which worker runs it, and the results are reproducible. Each task is one call to `bootstrap()`, and `mclapply()` runs them in parallel:

```{r}
#| label: r-mclapply
bootstrap <- function(seed, x, reps = 250) {
  set.seed(seed)
  replicate(reps, fit(sample(x, replace = TRUE)))
}

x <- c(-1.2, 0.3, 0.8, 1.1, 1.9, 2.4, 15)
estimates <- parallel::mclapply(1:4, bootstrap, x = x, mc.cores = 2)
estimates <- unlist(estimates)
length(estimates)
sd(estimates)
```

Nine of the 1,000 estimates are near 15. A search of the whole interval would have missed all nine and reported a standard error of 0.63, less than half the one above.

In R, `mclapply()` is `lapply()` spread over `mc.cores` processes. It relies on forking, so on Windows it runs only with `mc.cores = 1`; there, `parLapply()` with a cluster of separate R sessions does the same job.

Rust's standard library has no random number generator, so the Rust version uses the `rand` crate [@rand]. The factory and `minimize()` are the ones from @sec-closures, compiled but not shown, and `fit()` writes the grid search as a loop:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-threads
#| cargo: true
#| filename: src/main.rs
use rand::rngs::StdRng;
use rand::{RngExt, SeedableRng};
use std::thread;

# fn make_nll(data: Vec<f64>) -> impl Fn(f64) -> f64 {
#     move |m| {
#         let mut total = 0.0;
#         for x in &data {
#             total += (std::f64::consts::PI * (1.0 + (x - m).powi(2))).ln();
#         }
#         total
#     }
# }
#
# fn minimize(f: impl Fn(f64) -> f64, lower: f64, upper: f64) -> f64 {
#     let ratio = (5.0_f64.sqrt() - 1.0) / 2.0;
#     let mut a = lower;
#     let mut b = upper;
#     for _ in 0..60 {
#         let c = b - ratio * (b - a);
#         let d = a + ratio * (b - a);
#         if f(c) < f(d) {
#             b = d;
#         } else {
#             a = c;
#         }
#     }
#     (a + b) / 2.0
# }
#
fn fit(data: Vec<f64>) -> f64 {
    let nll = make_nll(data);
    let mut best = -10.0;
    for i in 1..=300 {
        let m = -10.0 + 0.1 * f64::from(i);
        if nll(m) < nll(best) {
            best = m;
        }
    }
    minimize(&nll, best - 0.1, best + 0.1)
}

fn bootstrap(data: &[f64], seed: u64, reps: u32) -> Vec<f64> {
    let mut rng = StdRng::seed_from_u64(seed);
    let mut estimates = Vec::new();
    for _ in 0..reps {
        // sample(data, replace = TRUE) in R
        let mut resample = Vec::new();
        for _ in 0..data.len() {
            resample.push(data[rng.random_range(0..data.len())]);
        }
        estimates.push(fit(resample));
    }
    estimates
}

fn sd(x: &[f64]) -> f64 {
    let n = x.len() as f64;
    let mean = x.iter().sum::<f64>() / n;
    let ss: f64 = x.iter().map(|v| (v - mean).powi(2)).sum();
    (ss / (n - 1.0)).sqrt()
}

fn main() {
    let x = vec![-1.2, 0.3, 0.8, 1.1, 1.9, 2.4, 15.0];
    let mut handles = Vec::new();
    for seed in 1..=4 {
        let x = x.clone();
        handles.push(thread::spawn(move || bootstrap(&x, seed, 250)));
    }

    let batches: Vec<Vec<f64>> = handles
        .into_iter()
        .map(|h| h.join().unwrap())
        .collect();
    let estimates = batches.concat();
    println!("{}", estimates.len());
    println!("{:.7}", sd(&estimates));
}
```

The function `StdRng::seed_from_u64()` creates a generator from a seed, like `set.seed()`, and `rng.random_range(0..data.len())` draws a position from that range, so each pass of the inner loop picks one element of `data` at random. Given the same resample, the two versions of `fit()` agree to four decimal places, so the standard errors differ only because the two languages use different generators; each is reproducible on its own. The `rand` documentation warns that `StdRng`'s algorithm may change in a future version of the crate and that its results may differ between platforms. A fixed `Cargo.lock` (@sec-crates) takes care of the first; for the same results on every platform, the documentation suggests the generator in the `chacha20` crate.

The function `thread::spawn()` starts a thread that runs a closure (@sec-closures) and returns a *join handle*. The thread may outlive the loop iteration that started it, so it can't borrow the loop's variables. With `move`, the closure gets its own copy of `seed` and its own clone of `x`, which is cheap for seven numbers; the next section shows threads that borrow instead.

Calling `h.join()` waits for a thread to finish and returns what its closure returned, inside a `Result` that's an error if the thread panicked. Collecting the handles first and joining them afterward lets the four tasks run at the same time; joining each one right after spawning it would run them one after another. Then `concat()` joins the four vectors into one, as `unlist()` does.

## Threads that borrow

A thread from `thread::spawn()` can't borrow local data from the code that started it, because it might still be running after that code has returned. A *scoped* thread can. The function `thread::scope()` waits for every thread started inside it before it returns, so those threads can borrow data from outside the scope:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-scoped
use std::thread;

fn main() {
    let data: Vec<u64> = (1..=1_000_000).collect();

    let total: u64 = thread::scope(|s| {
        let handles: Vec<_> = data
            .chunks(250_000)
            .map(|chunk| s.spawn(move || chunk.iter().sum::<u64>()))
            .collect();
        handles.into_iter().map(|h| h.join().unwrap()).sum()
    });

    println!("{total}");
    println!("{}", data.len());
}
```

The call `chunks(250_000)` splits the vector into slices of 250,000 elements (@sec-vectors), and each thread sums one slice. The slices borrow from `data`, so nothing is copied, and `data` is still usable afterward. The vector itself comes from `(1..=1_000_000).collect()`, which builds it from a range, like `1:1e6`.

::: {.callout-tip title="The same idea in R"}
The workers that `mclapply()` forks are separate processes, so a worker can't change anything in the session that started it:

```{r}
#| label: r-mclapply-isolated
total <- 0
invisible(parallel::mclapply(1:4, function(i) total <<- total + i,
                             mc.cores = 2))
total
```

Each worker changed its own copy of `total`. With `mc.cores = 1`, as on Windows, the calls run in the session itself, and `total` ends up 10. R gets safety from isolation and pays for it twice: in the memory a worker copies when it changes something, and in the cost of sending results back to the main session. Rust threads share memory, so they need rules about who can change what, and the rules are the ones from Part III.
:::

## Shared state

If threads could each add their part directly to one total, the result would depend on timing. Rust rejects that program. Spawning two scoped threads whose closures both run `total += ...` fails with "cannot borrow `total` as mutable more than once at a time", the rule from @sec-borrowing applied across threads. The usual fix is the one the examples above already used: each thread returns its result, and the main thread combines them.

When threads do need to change one value, it goes inside a `Mutex`, which lets one thread at a time lock the value, change it, and unlock it. A value shared by threads from `thread::spawn()` also needs an owner that all of them can hold. That's `Arc`, the thread-safe version of the reference-counted `Rc` from @sec-environments:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-arc-mutex
use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex};
use std::thread;

fn main() {
    let count = Arc::new(Mutex::new(0));
    let mut handles = Vec::new();
    for _ in 0..4 {
        let count = Arc::clone(&count);
        handles.push(thread::spawn(move || {
            *count.lock().unwrap() += 1;
        }));
    }
    for handle in handles {
        handle.join().unwrap();
    }
    println!("{}", *count.lock().unwrap());
}
```

Each thread gets its own `Arc` pointing to the same `Mutex`. Calling `lock()` waits until no other thread holds the lock, then returns a guard through which the value can be changed. It returns a `Result`, which is an error only if another thread panicked while holding the lock. The lock is released when the guard is dropped (@sec-drop), at the end of the statement here, so no thread can forget to unlock it.

The single-threaded `Rc` can't take the place of `Arc`. Moving an `Rc` into a spawned thread fails to compile with "`Rc<Vec<f64>>` cannot be sent between threads safely", because `Rc` updates its count without the synchronization `Arc` uses. The compiler tracks this with two traits: `Send` for types that can move to another thread, and `Sync` for types that threads can share references to [@rustbook, sec. 16.4]. Neither has to be implemented by hand; the compiler works them out from a type's fields.

::: {.callout-warning title="Where the analogy breaks"}
Rust prevents data races, but not every concurrency bug. Two threads that each wait for a lock the other holds will wait forever, a deadlock, and the compiler can't see that coming. The usual advice applies in both languages: share as little as possible, and prefer returning results to changing shared values.
:::

## Parallel iterators with `rayon`

In R, `mclapply()` is a parallel `lapply()`. In Rust, the `rayon` crate's parallel iterators are parallel versions of the iterators in @sec-iterators: change `iter()` to `par_iter()`, or `into_iter()` to `into_par_iter()`, and `rayon` spreads the work over a pool of threads:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-rayon
#| cargo: true
#| filename: src/main.rs
# use rand::rngs::StdRng;
# use rand::{RngExt, SeedableRng};
use rayon::prelude::*;
#
# fn make_nll(data: Vec<f64>) -> impl Fn(f64) -> f64 {
#     move |m| {
#         let mut total = 0.0;
#         for x in &data {
#             total += (std::f64::consts::PI * (1.0 + (x - m).powi(2))).ln();
#         }
#         total
#     }
# }
#
# fn minimize(f: impl Fn(f64) -> f64, lower: f64, upper: f64) -> f64 {
#     let ratio = (5.0_f64.sqrt() - 1.0) / 2.0;
#     let mut a = lower;
#     let mut b = upper;
#     for _ in 0..60 {
#         let c = b - ratio * (b - a);
#         let d = a + ratio * (b - a);
#         if f(c) < f(d) {
#             b = d;
#         } else {
#             a = c;
#         }
#     }
#     (a + b) / 2.0
# }
#
# fn fit(data: Vec<f64>) -> f64 {
#     let nll = make_nll(data);
#     let mut best = -10.0;
#     for i in 1..=300 {
#         let m = -10.0 + 0.1 * f64::from(i);
#         if nll(m) < nll(best) {
#             best = m;
#         }
#     }
#     minimize(&nll, best - 0.1, best + 0.1)
# }
#
# fn bootstrap(data: &[f64], seed: u64, reps: u32) -> Vec<f64> {
#     let mut rng = StdRng::seed_from_u64(seed);
#     let mut estimates = Vec::new();
#     for _ in 0..reps {
#         // sample(data, replace = TRUE) in R
#         let mut resample = Vec::new();
#         for _ in 0..data.len() {
#             resample.push(data[rng.random_range(0..data.len())]);
#         }
#         estimates.push(fit(resample));
#     }
#     estimates
# }
#
# fn sd(x: &[f64]) -> f64 {
#     let n = x.len() as f64;
#     let mean = x.iter().sum::<f64>() / n;
#     let ss: f64 = x.iter().map(|v| (v - mean).powi(2)).sum();
#     (ss / (n - 1.0)).sqrt()
# }

fn main() {
    let x = vec![-1.2, 0.3, 0.8, 1.1, 1.9, 2.4, 15.0];
    let batches: Vec<Vec<f64>> = (1..=4u64)
        .into_par_iter()
        .map(|seed| bootstrap(&x, seed, 250))
        .collect();
    println!("{:.7}", sd(&batches.concat()));
}
```

The functions are the ones from before, and the standard error is the same because the seeds are. The line `use rayon::prelude::*;` brings in the traits that add `into_par_iter()` and `par_iter()`; it's one of the few places where Rust code commonly uses `*` (@sec-crates). Here `collect()` keeps the results in their original order, as `mclapply()` does, however the work was divided. The crate decides how many threads to use, by default as many as the computer has CPUs available, and hands out work to them as they become free.

Unlike a thread from `thread::spawn()`, the closure passed to `map()` borrows `x`, with no clone. Like `thread::scope()`, a parallel iterator finishes every task before `collect()` returns, so nothing outlives the data it borrows.

The swap from `into_iter()` works because each task is independent. That closure must be safe to share between threads, so it can't change captured state the way an `FnMut` closure can; counting calls with `counted`, as @sec-closures did, wouldn't compile here. Each task returns its result instead, and `collect()` combines them.

Parallelism pays off only when each piece of work is large compared to the cost of handing it out. For small jobs, a plain iterator can be faster, so time both versions before keeping the parallel one, as you would before reaching for `mclapply()`.

## Summary

| R | Rust |
|---------------------------|---------------------------|
| `parallel::mclapply()`, `parLapply()` | `thread::spawn()`, `thread::scope()`, or `rayon` |
| Workers are separate processes | Threads share one process's memory |
| Results returned from each worker | Values returned from `join()` |
| Forked workers can't change the main session | Ownership and borrowing rule out data races |
| No shared state between workers | `Mutex` for shared changes, `Arc` for shared ownership |
| `set.seed()` in each parallel task | A seeded generator per task, from `rand` |
| `lapply()` to `mclapply()` | `iter()` to `par_iter()` |
| Not available with forking on Windows | The same code on every platform |
